pages.name: Welcome to Essence
pages.content:
Essence is a tabletop game about sharp, tactical combat and roleplay that stays entirely in your hands. When a fight breaks out, you'll manage dice pools, positioning, and a hand of cards that spell out exactly what your character can do. Outside of combat, the rules step back and your table drives the story.

This guide covers how to actually play a session from inside Foundry — your character sheet, rolling dice, and running combat through the tools this system gives you. For the full rules themselves, see the Combat Styles Reference journal and the Essence rulebook (v0.6).

Three Domains, No Classes

Every character is built from three domains — Physical (Might, Grace, Vigor), Mental (Intellect, Acuity, Resolve), and Spiritual (Presence, Adaptability, Anima). There's no class to pick. Your Attributes, Combat Styles, Species, Heritage, Distinction, and equipment combine into a character that's genuinely yours — two people who both invest in the same Combat Style can still play completely differently.

Where to Start

New to the sheet? Read Your Character Sheet next, then Combat once you're ready to fight. Everything else can wait until it comes up at the table.

pages.name: Your Character Sheet
pages.content:
Open your character from the Actors sidebar tab. Don't have one yet? Click Create Character, then open the wand icon in the sheet's header to launch the Character Creation Wizard — it walks you through Attributes, Career, Skills and Languages, Species/Heritage/Distinction, Combat Styles, cards and starting Equipment, and records your starting Advancement Points at the end.

Your sheet is split into tabs: Core (Attributes, Resources, Wounds, Death Track), Combat (Action/Reaction Cards and your Combat Style Specialties), Equipment (Inventory, Temporary, Armory), Non-Combat (Skills, Key Aspects, Reach and Influence, Connections), and Biography. Everything you need in a given moment lives on the relevant tab.

Your character belongs to a Team: a Team actor holds the group's Team Tier and record. Link to it from the Non-Combat tab. Team Tier governs which equipment Components are within ordinary access; it is not a rating of you or of your enemies.

pages.name: Attributes, Skills & Resources
pages.content:
Your 9 Attributes sit inside the three domains: Physical (Might, Grace, Vigor), Mental (Intellect, Acuity, Resolve), and Spiritual (Presence, Adaptability, Anima). Each domain also has a Resource you spend to act (Stamina, Focus, Mana) and a Defense others roll against to hit you (Fortitude, Composure, Harmony). A Defense is 2 plus the two lowest Attributes of its domain and never falls below 0.

Each domain covers three Combat Styles as well. Five of the nine — Gestalt, Magecraft, Psionics, Ritualism, and Calling — are gated: you need the matching Distinction before you can raise them above 0. Your sheet greys these out until you qualify. You start with five Expertises. Each Style holds at most its Rank in Expertises, and the Style tied to your Distinction holds one more.

Your base Action and Reaction Pools are 6 dice each, plus any explicit pool increase. Advancement is measured in Advancement Points (shown as Level on the sheet) spent through the Skill Tree.

pages.name: Attribute Benefits
pages.content:
Each Attribute also does something outside its dice pools. The sheet shows a one-line reminder under each Attribute; the rules in brief:

  • Might — carry 50 lb of exceptional cargo per point beyond personal equipment, with actual support and hands. Hauling doubles Movement cost.
  • Grace — running horizontal jump up to Grace units, with 2 units of run-up and a suitable landing.
  • Vigor — hold breath or sustain extreme effort for Vigor minutes (6 × Vigor Rounds) before the hazard procedure. Fatigued is the default strain Condition.
  • Intellect — 1 Non-Combat Skill Point per permanent point (creation maximum Rank 2, advancement maximum Rank 5).
  • Acuity — one primary language plus Acuity additional languages. Record them on the Non-Combat tab.
  • Resolve — sustain demanding attention for Resolve hours, then check each additional hour; failure normally causes Fatigued.
  • Presence — dependable personal allies as Connections, up to permanent Presence. The Non-Combat tab lists them.
  • Adaptability — once between Recoveries, after an Exploration task fails, reroll up to Adaptability dice together. The Core tab's checkbox tracks the use; Recovery restores it.
  • Anima — at each Recovery, after every Resource regains 25% rounded up, distribute Anima extra points among Stamina, Focus and Mana.

Temporary Attribute changes never grant Skill Points, languages or Connections.

pages.name: Rolling Dice
pages.content:
Click a Non-Combat Skill, Attribute or Key Aspect to roll it. Outside combat the pool is Attribute + Skill Rank (or Attribute + 5 for a Key Aspect). The GM sets a Difficulty from 1 to 10; your highest die must meet it. If the GM leaves it blank the roll posts open and the GM reads the highest die.

In combat, playing an Action or Reaction Card spends from a pool instead — your Action Dice on your own Turn, your Reaction Dice on everyone else's. You choose how many dice to commit (at least the card's minimum — never fewer than 2 — up to whatever's left in the pool); the sheet warns when you exceed the card's normal maximum of Attribute + Style Rank (floored at 2 for Basic and Rank 0 cards). Some costs are burned rather than rolled: Dash burns 2, Reconfigure and Stabilize burn 3, and a card's text can add a burned die. Burned dice never roll.

Your highest rolled die is your Success Die, compared against the target's Defense. Every other rolled die that shows 6 or higher generates a Surge, which you spend on the options printed on the card. More dice means better odds and more Surges, but fewer dice left for whatever happens next.

pages.name: Wounds & Recovery
pages.content:
Essence doesn't use a hit point bar. Apply Damage on the Core tab takes a hit as printed: up to three components, each with an amount and a Damage type, plus Breach or nonlethal flags and any flat reduction. Components resolve in order. Each first meets your Resistance or Vulnerability to that type, then your Resilience (a buffer that resets at the start of each of your Turns; Breach ignores it), then any Temporary Wounds, and only then fills a Core Wound space. You have 5 Core spaces, filled in order: 2 Light, 2 Serious, then 1 Critical. Each filled space attaches a Wound Card for the Damage type's domain (Physical, Mental or Spiritual) with its ongoing effect.

Your Wound State follows the highest-severity space filled. When the fifth space fills you are Dying: the Death Track advances at the start of each of your Turns, and acting while Dying pushes it once more per Round. Reaching the end is death, and death is final. Stabilize (a Basic Action, burn 3) stops the advance if its treatment requirements are met; a nonlethal hit that fills the track leaves you Stabilized and unconscious instead of Dying. Opening any Core space ends the incapacity.

Recovery

When the GM grants a Recovery, click Grant Recovery. Each Resource regains 25% of its maximum rounded up (halved and rounded up again while Fatigued), then Anima extra points go wherever you choose. The dialog lists your filled Core Wounds so you tick the ones whose Wound Card requirements were met: Light Wounds usually clear with care and one Recovery, Serious Wounds need post-Adventure Downtime, and a Critical Wound normally needs four weeks of appropriate Downtime care (twenty-eight qualifying days). Recovery also reduces the Death Track by 1 when you are not Dying, clears Psionic Strain, removes 1 Manifestation Wound, and restores the Adaptability reroll. It never restores Temporary Wounds or Temporary Influence.

pages.name: Combat
pages.content:
Combat runs through Foundry's own Combat Tracker. When the GM starts an encounter, roll Initiative from your sheet or the tracker: commit from 1 die up to your base Action Pool. Those dice are rolled and totalled for turn order, and whatever you did not commit becomes extra Action Dice on your first Turn (ties break by the higher Success Die, then Grace).

At the start of your Turn the tracker clears your Reaction Pool, discards any prepared Action and its reserved dice, resets accumulated Damage, forms your Action Pool and applies Dazed's burn. Spend Action Dice on cards, Movement (burn 1 die per extra unit) and Basic Actions. Click End Turn to settle end-of-Turn steps (Gestalt upkeep, Combo) and convert whatever's left into your Reaction Pool: base pool plus unspent Action Dice.

Prepare Action (burn 2, then reserve dice) holds one Action for a trigger before your next Turn; the sheet shows a Fire button while it is held. A prepared Action or a Reaction uses your one response in a chain. Cards with a cooldown re-enable once per Round automatically, or once per Encounter when someone clicks New Encounter — ending one Combat in Foundry does not end the fictional Encounter.

pages.name: Combat Style Specialties
pages.content:
Every Combat Style has its own thing to track, and the Combat tab shows the tracker for each Style you have:

  • Prowess — Combo pips (max 5, each +1 Movement) and a "dealt Damage this Turn" tick; End Turn drops 1 Combo when it is clear.
  • Ballistics — Establish Lock burns 1 Action die and records the target (two Locks with the Marksman Origin).
  • Gestalt — your Adaptation and its upkeep, paid automatically at End Turn or the Adaptation ends. Tick "assumed outside my Turn" to defer the first payment.
  • Cunning — Contingencies (one per Round, two with the Strategist), with a Trigger button; unused ones expire at your next Turn.
  • Magecraft — Threads: click a subtype to create one after its Action, hold up to 3 (duplicates allowed), consume from the list before a roll.
  • Psionics — Strain: the dice prompt offers 1 Strain for a free Surge; Vent burns 2 for 2; forced Strain past 6 becomes Breach Damage.
  • Leadership — Authority stored per card (two results per card for an Orator); click a result to spend it.
  • Ritualism — Rites with Trigger, Echo, Echo Limit and Possessed subject; three (four for an Invoker).
  • Calling — the shared five-space Manifestation Wound track and the header-menu entry into Full Manifestation. See the Full Manifestation Guide.

Everything that ends with the Encounter clears when a GM clicks New Encounter. See the Combat Styles Reference journal for each Style's full rules, Expertises and subtypes.

pages.name: Adventures & Downtime
pages.content:
Play moves Planning → Adventure → Downtime → Planning. An Adventure ends when its central undertaking is resolved, abandoned, made impossible or transformed. Complete success is only one ending.

What an Adventure ending resets

Click New Adventure on your sheet once the table agrees the Adventure is over. It releases what is measured across the Adventure: Reach pressure, Adventure-limited Reach Triggers, and Uses that recover "at the end of the Adventure" (Augments and Equipment Cards whose own rule says so). Your Inventory allocation is released too, so you can choose a new Inventory the next time you reach your Armory. Temporary Influence from grants that have expired is removed.

An Adventure ending does not restore Stamina, Focus or Mana, heal Core Wounds, clear Core Influence, refill Consumable Kits, or repair lost equipment. Those follow Recovery, resupply and their own rules.

Downtime

Downtime has no fixed length and can hold one Recovery or several; the GM applies them. Critical Wounds count elapsed qualifying days of care during Downtime (four weeks by default). Retraining and Skill Tree purchases happen here as well. The Adventure's end also settles the Armory: keep what fits your Armory Limit, and sell, trade, return or discard the rest.

pages.name: Setting Up NPCs
pages.content:
Create an enemy from the Actors sidebar's Create Actor button with Type set to NPC / Adversary (or Monster, which adds the Monster Creator). Every enemy has a Grade — Mook, Normal or Elite — and a battlefield Role (Defender, Striker, Controller, Blaster, Support, Skirmisher). Grade decides how the enemy is run:

  • Mooks and Normals use the reduced engine: no dice Pools and no Resources. Their sheet is a compact record — Grade, Role, Wounds, printed Defenses, Resilience, Movement, Senses and Abilities — plus their printed allowances: Initiative dice (2d10), Actions per Turn (Mook 1, Normal 2), Reactions per Round and Task Dice (4 or 5). Leave an allowance blank to use the Grade default. A GM toggle reveals Attributes, Styles and cards for hand-building.
  • Elites use the full engine like a character: Pools of 6, printed card costs, and an optional printed Roll Limit.

Abilities are the enemy's printed moves. Each has a kind (Action, Reaction, Triggered or Passive), its printed dice, the Defense it rolls against or an unopposed flag, and a frequency: At Will, once per Round, or a number of uses between Recoveries. The Recovery button refreshes limited uses; nothing else does, not even a new Combat.

The Starting Enemy Examples compendium holds the ten playtest profiles from the rulebook (three Mooks, four Normals, three Elites). Import one and change its fiction freely.

Leave enemy tokens unlinked (Foundry's default) so several copies track their own Wounds. Character tokens are force-linked instead.

Portrait Art vs. Token Art

Every Actor has two images: the sheet Portrait (click the header art) and the canvas Token Image (the pawn icon on the Portrait's corner). Foundry copies the Portrait into the Token Image the first time you set one; after that they are independent. Since enemy tokens are unlinked, a new Token Image only affects tokens placed afterwards.

pages.name: Enemy Construction
pages.content:
Enemies are compact profiles, not characters. Wound capacity by Grade: Mook 2, Normal 4, Elite 5. All three are Defeated when their capacity fills; they use no severity spaces, Wound Cards or Death Track. A Defeated enemy is unconscious and dying unless Stabilize or a nonlethal hit made it stable (the header reads "Defeated (stable)").

Reduced engine (Mooks and Normals)

Initiative is a plain 2d10 roll, made automatically when you roll from the tracker. Each Turn grants the printed Actions; each Round the printed Reactions, refreshed at the start of every Round. Abilities roll their printed dice against the named Defense with the normal Success Die and Surges. There are no Pools, so Dazed's burn and the unaware surcharge are waived. One utility Basic Action per Turn (Dash, Reconfigure, Stabilize or Perform Task, including Help) spends an Action and costs no dice. Basic Melee Attack, Basic Ranged Attack, Defend and Prepare Action need explicit permission, so the sheet refuses them and the Monster Creator never picks them. For an uncertain task, Roll Task Dice against a Difficulty. The sheet warns when an allowance is exceeded rather than blocking, since profiles control exceptions.

Elites

Elites pay card costs from Pools. An ability's printed dice are its minimum commitment, paid through the usual prompt with the profile's Roll Limit shown as advice. Task Dice fall back to the Roll Limit.

Planning

Encounter categories by target length: Minor 1–2 Rounds, Severe 2–3, Critical 3–5, Boss usually 3–5 with a Leader or Solo structure. A short Adventure has about 1–2 meaningful combats, a medium one 2–4, a long one 4–6 or more separated by Recovery opportunities. Team Tier is not an enemy rating; pick opposition for the story.

pages.name: Running Combat
pages.content:
Combat runs entirely through Foundry's own Combat Tracker — add combatants, click Begin Combat, and advance rounds and turns from there. Every way of rolling Initiative opens the same commit prompt for characters and Elites (1 die up to the base pool); Mooks and Normals roll 2d10 with no prompt. Combatants sort by total, then Success Die, then Grace.

The tracker runs each Turn's bookkeeping: Pools form and clear, prepared Actions expire, accumulated Damage resets, Dazed burns, reduced-engine allowances refresh, and the Death Track advances for a Dying character. End of Turn settles Gestalt upkeep and Combo, then forms the Reaction Pool.

Deleting the Combat does not end the fictional Encounter: anything scoped to the Encounter — Threads, Authority, Locks, Combo, Contingencies, Stance and Unstable, per-Encounter Card cooldowns, an active Full Manifestation — stays until a sheet's own New Encounter button is clicked. Use it once the table agrees the Encounter, not just one bout of Combat, is over.

pages.name: Conditions & Content
pages.content:
Conditions live in the Conditions compendium and double as Token HUD status icons — right-click a token, open its status-effects palette, and toggle a Condition directly. This adds or removes a real owned Condition item on the Actor with its mechanical effect (Exposed's −1 to all Defenses, for instance), exactly the same as dragging the Condition onto the sheet. The sheet's + Add button on the Conditions row does the same from a picker. Each Condition Item carries a Classification (Ordinary/Specialty/Wound/Influence Consequence/Cover/Other) purely as a label.

Stacking, Reapplication, and Participation

Differently named Conditions stack. The same named ordinary Condition does not stack with itself — reapplying it refreshes or extends its duration without shortening what remains. Ordinary Condition removal never removes a Wound Card, a Specialty Condition, Strain or Manifestation Wounds unless it explicitly says it can. A Condition restricts only what its own entry names; the character keeps their remaining Actions, Reactions and Movement.

Authoring New Content

If you have Foundry's "Create Items" permission, a wand-icon scene-control button opens the Create Content wizard for building new Action/Reaction Cards, Equipment, and Conditions straight into the compendium. For adding many at once, use its Bulk Import option: download a CSV template, fill it out, and upload it.

Compendiums

Species, Heritages, Distinctions, the Starting Enemy Examples and the Full Manifestation profiles are hand-authored from the v0.6 rulebook. The Combat Styles Reference and Full Manifestation Guide journals document their mechanics in full.

pages.name: Grade Budgets
pages.content:
The Monster Creator's Auto-Generate Stat Block button fills a hand-built Elite (or a full-stats Mook or Normal) from a tunable budget table, then hands every result back for you to edit. Defaults match the rulebook's Starting Enemy Examples:

Mook2 pts, max 22 pts, max 2001 / 012
Normal7 pts, max 35 pts, max 3102 / 124
Elite13 pts, max 512 pts, max 5204 / 345

Auto-Generate rolls, in order: a weighted Attribute/Style point-buy (leaning toward the domain you pick as Emphasis and respecting the five Distinction gates), Resilience and Temporary Wounds from the table, qualifying Combat Cards weighted toward the highest Styles (never Basic Melee Attack, Basic Ranged Attack, Defend or Prepare Action, which enemies need permission for), and a random Equipment draw. Each step has its own Reroll button.

Treat the table as a starting point — the examples run Resilience 0 for Mooks, 1–2 for Normals and 2–3 for Elites. Every number is in the Grade Budgets system setting and takes effect immediately.

pages.name: Team Tier & Economic Scale
pages.content:
Create one Team actor per party and link each character to it. The Team sheet holds Team Tier (1 to 5) and the Team record: identity, Major Goal, methods and principles; Things and Commitments tagged Asset, Obligation, Borrowed or Pledged; and Organizations as Friendly, Neutral or Hostile. Track what matters at the current scale, not every possession.

Team Tier is lasting Campaign progression and only increases, when you judge the Campaign ready for a broader scope. There is no point threshold. Raising it on the Team sheet clears every member's remaining Temporary Influence; it refunds no spent Influence, clears no Core consequences, and grants no personal dice, cards or capacity. Tier never rates a character's competence or an enemy's strength.

Acquisition

Through routine channels a character can obtain a Chassis or Fitting whose Component Tier is no higher than Team Tier (each Component checked separately, up to Tier 5) when a supplier exists. The Equipment tab flags Components above the Team's Tier as exceptional; obtained gear is always usable and keeps no rent. Personal Reach absorbs the Influence pressure of a significant acquisition; it does not by itself open higher-Tier suppliers. Quartermaster's Due grants one Chassis and one Fitting up to 1 Tier above Team Tier at creation.

Judging scale

Use these reference anchors for a noticeable expense: Tier 1 about $100, Tier 2 $1,000, Tier 3 $10,000, Tier 4 $100,000, Tier 5 $1,000,000. Routine expenses below the scale create no pressure; a meaningful one near the anchor is 1 ordinary pressure; a heavier commitment can be several. Printed Influence costs keep their stated amounts at every Tier.

pages.name: What Full Manifestation Is
pages.content:
Calling represents a bond between your character and a supernatural entity — a spirit, ancestor, or other manifested power. Most Calling cards channel only a piece of that bond. You stay in play, playing yourself.

Full Manifestation is the Style's fixed Rider: your character steps aside and the form takes their place on the battlefield, using its own Defenses, Resilience, Movement, Senses, Roll Limit and granted Actions and Reactions. You are not gaining a second creature; you disappear, and it stands where you were, as the same character for Initiative, Turn and Reaction-chain purposes.

Forms come in fixed families by Rank: Familiar and Sprite at Rank 0; Beast, Phantom and Golem at Rank 1; Elemental, Ancestor and Fey at Rank 2 (Ranks 3 to 5 name Dragon, Fiend, Celestial, Abomination, Leviathan, Avatar, Outsider, Titan and Primordial, without profiles yet). The rulebook supplies no numeric profiles in this edition; the eight in the Calling Full Manifestations compendium are Campaign-supplied playtest profiles.

pages.name: Entering a Full Manifestation
pages.content:
Play an eligible Calling Action as normal and pay its printed cost. Then open your sheet's header menu and choose Full Manifestation. Each form in the list shows the Rider's surcharge, which is paid automatically when you enter: extra burned Action dice and extra Mana by the form's Rank.

The Summoner's Greater Manifestation reduces only the burned-die surcharge by 1. The underlying card still costs its full minimum, at least 2 Pool dice. You need the dice available; short Mana warns. You cannot enter while Broken, and you must return before entering another form.

pages.name: While You're Manifested
pages.content:
You aren't getting a fresh Turn. The form picks up exactly where you left off: your remaining Action and Reaction Dice are all it has, Movement already spent stays spent, and the response you used in a chain stays used. Your own Wounds, Conditions, Death Track and durations pause underneath — manifesting heals nothing.

Your card options shrink to the form's own granted Actions and Reactions; universal Basics, your learned cards and Species or Equipment Actions are not inherited unless the profile says so. Native cards use the Rank's minimum commitment (the form's sheet enforces it) and the form's printed Roll Limit as their maximum; Mana costs come out of your own Mana. Prepared Actions still expire on schedule.

To leave, click Return (burn 1) on the form's sheet during your Turn: 1 Action die is burned, your token swaps back, and the form's Conditions and Temporary Wounds end. The form otherwise stays until it collapses, the Encounter ends (New Encounter returns you for free), or an effect ends it.

pages.name: Damage, Wounds & Defeat
pages.content:
All of your forms share one five-space Manifestation Wound track, shown as pips in the Calling row of your Combat tab. When you enter a form, its sheet shows that track as it stands; Wounds it takes fill the shared track, and they stay filled when you return and when you enter another form later. Manifestation Wounds cause no Wound Cards for you. The active form uses its own Resilience and any Temporary Wounds it gains; your paused Wounds never transfer.

Apply Damage on the form's sheet resolves each component in order. Your accumulated ordinary Damage carries into the form and back, so switching bodies never shrugs off a hit that already landed.

Collapse and Broken

When a component fills the fifth space, the form collapses at once. The rest of that component's Wounds are discarded, your token returns, and you directly suffer 1 Spiritual Core Wound that bypasses Resilience, Resistance and Temporary Wounds (a full Core track advances the Death Track instead). Any later components of that hit are posted to chat for the GM to recheck against you by hand. The shared track stays full and you are Broken: no Full Manifestation, though ordinary Calling cards still work. Each Recovery removes 1 Manifestation Wound, and removing one from a full track ends Broken. The pips on your sheet can also be adjusted by hand.

Every profile shares the caller's five-space Manifestation Wound track, so no profile has a Wound capacity of its own. A profile marked Living is a valid target for a living-only effect; one marked Nonliving is not — but it still feels pain, can be restrained, and is affected by mental attacks, magic, and ordinary Conditions. Being a Phantom doesn't make you incorporeal.

Open any profile from the Calling Full Manifestations compendium to read its stat block and maneuvers. These are Campaign-supplied playtest profiles; the GM may add a Roll Limit in the header.

pages.name: For Game Masters
pages.content:
The first time a character fully manifests a given subtype, the system creates that character's own persistent copy of the profile and gives the controlling player Owner permission on it — you don't need to drag anything from the compendium. Later manifestations of the same subtype reuse that copy.

Entering, returning and collapse are one click each: the entry surcharge is deducted, the token swaps, and the shared Manifestation Wound track is copied in and written back. Collapse applies the caller's direct Spiritual Core Wound and its Wound Card and marks the caller Broken. What stays by hand: rechecking any later Damage components of a collapsing hit against the returned caller (posted to chat), and judging whether the form fits its space when it appears or returns.

If a track was filled by hand-toggled pips rather than Apply Damage, the form's header menu offers Collapse (track full) to run the same collapse.
